Subject: [geomorph-r-package] Test with phylosig and kmult

Hello everyone,

I am measuring phylogenetic signal (K) for a multivariate dataset and I tried the phylosig in geomorph and the Kmult function in phylocurve, but I am having trouble interpreting the results. Both K values are the same with both functions, but the null distributions compared against are different. I read and they do randomise different things, so it makes sense that they are different. But could anyone help me interpret what both tests are saying?

My results are: Observed K=0.13, P= 0.03 for geomorph, P=0.04 for phylocurve.  For geomorph the observed K is to the right of the null distribution of Ks and for phylocurve the K is to the left of the null distribution, in this case the null distribution goes from 0.5 to 1.5.

Thank you very much!

Best,

Iliana

Hi Dean,
I've been struggling to get this code to work and plot the group allometries (in different colors and with different regression lines). I can get procD.lm to produce results but the plot seems to be allometry-free, which seems appropriate given the example explanations. Any suggestions are appreciated. Here's my code.

library(devtools) #improved geomorph is not yet approved by CRAN
devtools::install_github("geomorphR/geomorph",ref="Stable")
library(geomorph)

setwd("D:/Documents/Analysis IV/MJ fewer LMs")

FFPEntire<-readland.tps("IV FFP 164 Entire 34 LMs.TPS", specID = "ID")

groups<-read.csv("R_FFP_Entire_Base_Classifiers.csv",header=TRUE,stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
type<-as.factor(groups$TypeE5)
Y.gpa<-gpagen(FFPEntire)

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa)

FFPEntireAllometry <- procD.allometry(coords~Csize, ~type,
                                      logsz = TRUE, data=gdf, iter=10000, RRPP=TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)

FFPEntANOVA <- procD.lm(FFPEntireAllometry$formula, data = FFPEntireAllometry$data, iter = 999,
                        RRPP = TRUE, print.progress = FALSE)

summary(FFPEntANOVA)

plot(FFPEntireAllometry, method="RegScore")

plot(FFPEntANOVA, type = "regression",
     predictor = log(gdf$Csize),
     reg.type = "RegScore",
     pch = 21,
     bg = as.numeric(gdf$Treatment),
     xlab = "log(CS)")

Thanks,
Dave

messages.subject: digitsuface function placing surface semilandmarks undesirably
messages.subject_clean: digitsuface function placing surface semilandmarks undesirably
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am doing GMM on 3D dataset. I digitized a template using IDAV Landmark Editor. In this template, there are 5 landmarks, 20 curve semilandmarks, and 50 surface semilandmarks (Template_lmclmslm.nts file).

The following code can be used to view my template:

library(geomorph)

template_ply <- read.ply("C:\\Users\\<username>\\Desktop\\Template_vertices.ply")

lmks_template <- readland.nts("C:\\Users\\<username>\\Desktop\\Template_lmclmslm.nts")

plot3d(lmks_template[1:6,,1], type = "s", radius = 1.5, col = "red", aspect = FALSE, add = T)

plot3d(lmks_template[7:26,,1], type = "s", radius = 1.5, col = "blue", aspect = FALSE, add = T)

plot3d(lmks_template[27:76,,1], type = "s", radius = 1.5, col = "yellow", aspect = FALSE, add = T)

The resultant image is displayed as below (red landmarks, blue curve semilandmars, and yellow surface semilandmarks):

I wish to apply this template to my sample to let digitsurface function place surface semilandmarks on the sample for me. To accomplish this task, I used the following code:

open3d()

sample_ply <- read.ply("C:\\Users\\<username>\\Desktop\\Sample_vertices.ply")

lmks_sample <- readland.nts("C:\\Users\\<username>\\Desktop\\Sample_lmclm.nts")

digitsurface(sample_ply, fixed = lmks_sample[,,1], ptsize = 1, center = TRUE)

Note that lmks_sample[,,1] contains 6 landmarks and 20 curve semilandmarks. But I treat all 26 points as fixed landmarks at this stage. They will only be differentiated during GPA. I did it this way because geomorph tutorial allowed this.

Unfortunately, the resultant images is shown as below, which indicates that the semilandmarks are not placed in similar locations as they are placed in the template. Even the landmarks (red) of the sample are severely displaced.

I double checked the correctness of the landmarks of my sample using the following code:

open3d()

plot3d(sample_ply)

plot3d(lmks_sample[1:6,,1], type = "s", radius = 1.5, col = "red", aspect = FALSE, add = T)

plot3d(lmks_sample[7:26,,1], type = "s", radius = 1.5, col = "blue", aspect = FALSE, add = T)

The resultant image is shown below:

All landmarks (including real fixed landmarks and curve semilandmarks which are treated as fixed landmarks) are correctly positioned, suggesting that there should be no issue with the lmks_sample data fed to the fixed argument in digitsurface function.

I checked previous posts in this forum and noted two possible causes:

1. Lou indicated that "lumps of triangle summits in the same areas where digitsurface lumped semi-landmarks together" could be the reason and "non-decimated mesh with regularly spaced vertices to build the template helped correct this issue" (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/geomorph-r-package/digitsurface|sort:date/geomorph-r-package/_RqlvyC8LQ4/UvIbL7VZBQAJ <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/geomorph-r-package/digitsurface%7Csort:date/geomorph-r-package/_RqlvyC8LQ4/UvIbL7VZBQAJ>). But I checked my mesh in MeshLab and did not seem to note lumped triangles.

2. Sherratt suggested that "specimen lack homologous points (fixed landmarks)" could be another reason (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/geomorph-r-package/digitsurface|sort:date/geomorph-r-package/yu4UyOhqZqc/X5kadFj3AAAJ <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/geomorph-r-package/digitsurface%7Csort:date/geomorph-r-package/yu4UyOhqZqc/X5kadFj3AAAJ>). At first, I thought this could be an issue since I treated 20 curve semilandmarks as fixed landmarks. But the isssue did not resolve even I only used the 6 landmarks by specifying fixed = lmks_sample[1:6,,1] in the digitsurface function.

Original data with explanations of their contents are available via GitHub (https://github.com/Patricklv/digitsurface-function-question) so that with the code above, my errors could be replicated. I wish to know what should I do so that surface semilandmarks could be placed on my sample in roughly corresponding places as they are placed on my template.

Thanks.

You did not follow the instructions in the help file. The example using procD.lm shows the original variables being added:

## From help file:

data(larvalMorph)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(larvalMorph$tailcoords, curves = larvalMorph$tail.sliders, print.progress = FALSE)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, Treatment = larvalMorph$treatment,
Family = larvalMorph$family)

# procD.lm approach, including interaction
tailAllometry2 <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) * Treatment, data = gdf, iter = 149,
     print.progress = FALSE)
plot(tailAllometry2, type = "regression",
predictor = log(gdf$Csize),
reg.type = "PredLine",

pch = 21,
bg = as.numeric(gdf$Treatment),

xlab = "log(CS)") # greater flexibility

If you follow precisely what shown in the help file that should get you closer to your goal.

Dean

Thank you very much for your suggestions of this alternative. I have also noted that such template registration work could be done using other software, Landmark Editor is surely one of them. I wish to do it in geomorph since I have a large dataset and wish to be more efficient.

Regarding the .ply files you mentioned, as far as I know, geomorph requires ascii ply format, which is the format I have. I am not sure if there is any other additional requirement regarding the ply file.

By the way, I tried to increase the number of surface semilandmarks (~3000) in my template, which unfortunately did not seem to have any effect of the location of surface semilandmarks placed on the sample (image shown below). I tried to dive into the source code for the digitsurface function but did not figure out where along the algorithm went wrong.

Thank you!

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone, I want to create a different deformation grids for each species I'm examining; how the average of each species changes from the overall average (all species combined). I would like to interpret the shape changes and describe certain areas as wider, longer, etc. I've utilized some code I found here, but seem to be getting stuck. I've used the plethodon dataset as an example so it's clear what it being done.

When I utilize code I found on this group's page I seem to only get a flat grid with no warping. I've attached a photo of the grid. I get a grid with no warping using my data as well. My first thought it that there is so little change that I'm not getting warping in the grid.

data(plethodon)
Y.gpa<-gpagen(plethodon$land)
coords.jord <- Y.gpa$coords[,,plethodon$species=="Jord"]
mean.jord <- mshape(coords.jord)
grand.mean <- mshape(Y.gpa$coords)
plotRefToTarget(grand.mean, mean.jord, method="TPS")

That's my first problem.  My second problem is I want to add vector arrows as well, but I can't seem to figure out how to. I just get arrows pointing back at my points.

arrows(grand.mean[,1],grand.mean[,2],mean.jord[,1],mean.jord[,2],length=0.1,lwd=2)

I also have another question about grid interpretation. If I have species A as reference and species B as target, can I use that grid to interpret shape changes, like species B is wider than species A?

I've been trying to find help on this for a while and keep getting stuck. Sorry for the basic questions, I'm newer to R and still learning.

messages.body_plain:
Lindsay,

the example code you sent does what it should, and produces "deformed" grids. Maybe they are not too visible because the amount of shape change is small. Try exaggerating it a bit by using:
plotRefToTarget(grand.mean, mean.jord, method="TPS", mag=5)

You can make a vectors plot by using:

 plotRefToTarget(grand.mean, mean.jord, method="vector", mag=5)

If you want to have both the grid and the vectors, you will have to do that by hand, as geomorph does not provide that plotting option. I believe the Practical Companion Mimi Zelditch sent out some days ago includes an example on that, you can find the post here: plotRefToTarget(grand.mean, mean.jord, method="TPS", mag=5)

As for interpretation, it sounds like you have got it right, if what you are seeing are arrows making the structure wider as you move from A to B.

Hope this helps,
Antigoni

To add to what Antigoni wrote: the default for the method="TPS" is to show the landmarks of the target form, and you drew the vectors from the reference to the target; because the change is so slight, the arrowheads overlap the landmarks. If you exaggerate the change by 5, you will also need to lengthen the arrows, so you'd need to calculate the coordinates for the new target. If you call the target for the exaggerated change "jord.exag", that would be
jord.exag=grand.mean+5*(mean.jord-grand.mean)

When you look at the result, you can decide whether to show the landmarks where the arrows point, or at the base of the arrow so the arrows are pointing away from them to the landmarks of the target. It you'd prefer the second, add UseRefPts=T to the argument for the deformed grid).
We have a chapter on graphics in the revised Practical Companion, but I don't think that we discussed how to get the coordinates of the target form for a magnified change.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have some problems figuring out if I am using the ProCD.lm function correctly and getting the right out of it.

I am testing whether there are any size and shape differences between males and females in one population of animals. I have microscribed 31 landmarks on the skulls, and converted them to a TPS format, and used the readland.tps to put the data into R:

> mydata <- readland.tps("Skulls", specID ="ID")

I added a separate document containing one column with the IDs and one with the ID "Sex" telling if they are female or male.

> classifier <- read.csv("Classifier.csv", header=TRUE, row.name <http://row.name>=1, sep="\t")

I did a GPA:

> gpa <- gpagen(mydata, PrinAxes = TRUE, ProcD = TRUE, Proj = TRUE, print.progress = TRUE)

And a PCA:

> gp <- interaction(classifier$Sex)
> PCA_skulls <- plotTangentSpace(gpa$coords, groups = gp)

Then I wanted to test if males and females are different in size or shape.
I made a dataframe:

> gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape=gpa$coords, size=gpa$Csize, sex=classifier$Sex)

And from here I start questioning myself if I am during it correctly. I am using the proCD.lm function.

I took the size and shape separately:

> gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape=gpa$coords, size=gpa$Csize, sex=classifier$Sex)

> myresults<-procD.lm(shape~sex, data = gdf)
> myresults2<-procD.lm(size~sex, data = gdf)

And got this for shape:
> procD.lm(f1 = shape ~ sex, data = gdf)
>
> Type I (Sequential) Sums of Squares and Cross-products
> Randomized Residual Permutation Procedure Used
> 1000 Permutations
> ANOVA effect sizes and P-values based on empirical F distributions
>
>                 Df      SS       MS               Rsq      F         Z         Pr(>F)
> sex           1    0.08868 0.088681 0.25081 25.443 5.9886  0.001 **
> Residuals 76  0.26490 0.003485 0.74919
> Total         77  0.35358
> ---
> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

And this for size:
> procD.lm(f1 = size ~ sex, data = gdf)
>
> Type I (Sequential) Sums of Squares and Cross-products
> Randomized Residual Permutation Procedure Used
> 1000 Permutations
> ANOVA effect sizes and P-values based on empirical F distributions
>
>                   Df     SS          MS     Rsq            F         Z        Pr(>F)
> sex            1    145084 145084 0.75485    234.01 3.0314  0.001 **
> Residuals 76   47119    620       0.24515
> Total           77 192204
> ---
> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

However, I do not know if this is the correct way of during it, or if I should have the size and shape into one equation? And if it actually is testing whether females and males are different?

Thanks,

Julie

Geometric morphometrics using R (GMMR02)

https://www.prstatistics.com/course/geometric-morphometrics-using-r-gmmr02/

Please feel free to share!

This course will be delivered by Dean Adams, Mike Collyer and Antigoni Kaliontzopoulou in Glasgow City Centre for the 30th September - 4th October 2019

You will recognise these names from answering many of the questions on morphmet and as the developers of Geomorph - you could not ask for a better combinations of instructors!

Course overview:
The field of geometric morphometrics (GM) is concerned with the quantification and analysis of patterns of shape variation, and its covariation with other variables. Over the past several decades these approaches have become a mainstay in the field of ecology, evolutionary biology, and anthropology, and a panoply of analytical tools for addressing specific biological hypotheses concerning shape have been developed. The goal of this is to provide participants with a working knowledge of the theory of geometric morphometrics, as well as practical training in the application of these methods.

The course is organized in both theoretical and practical sessions. The theoretical sessions will provide a comprehensive introduction to the methods of landmark-based geometric morphometrics, which aims at providing the participants with a solid theoretical background for understanding the procedures used in shape data analysis. Practical sessions will include worked examples, giving the participants the opportunity to gain hands-on experience in the treatment of shape data using the R package geomorph. These sessions focus on the generation of shape variables from primary landmark data, the statistical treatment of shape variation with respect to biological hypotheses, and the visualization of patterns of shape variation and of the shapes themselves for interpretation of statistical findings, using the R language for statistical programming. While practice datasets will be available, it is strongly recommended that participants come with their own datasets.

Note: Because this is a geometric morphometrics workshop in R, it is assumed, and is in fact required, that participants have some working knowledge in R. The practical sessions of the course will focus on GM-based analyses, and not basic R user-interfacing. It is therefore strongly recommended that participants refresh their R skills prior to attending the workshop.

Eve,

The model.comparison function in the RRPP package might be appealing.  You can still perform AIC, but you have other options.  Additionally, the anova function via RRPP (anova.lm.rrpp) functions like a likelihood ratio test for multiple models.  Examples are provided in the help pages, and there is a vignette.  I recommend installing from github to get the most up-to-date version, i.e.,

devtools::install_github(“mlcollyer/RRPP”)

Both RRPP and geomorph use the same RRPP framework, but RRPP is more bare bones whereas geomorph is more morphometric-focused.

If you wish to stay within geomorph, the advanced.procD.lm function can compare two models.  You could do a few pairwise model comparisons, test by test.  The anova.lm.rrpp function uses the same concept, but allows for more models, and has additional output (like confidence intervals for test statistics).

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.subject: Phylogenetic methods for shape variables
messages.body_plain:
What are currently viewed as the best practices for using shape variables to construct phylogenetic hypotheses? I’ve read a number of different methods in the literature and understand the limitations/issues with the applications, but admittedly lack the background to assess best (least worst?) options. The common options I’ve encountered include:

Neighbor joining on Procrustes distances
Maximum likelihood of continuous characters (PC scores, LDA scores, regular or transformed)
Weighted parsimony of scaled measurements

I’m specifically asking for extinct taxa where no molecular hypotheses exist, and taxa where continuous characters are more applicable than codeable ones. TIA.

Russ

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Phylogenetic methods for shape variables
messages.body_plain:
Russ,

Under NO circumstances should one transform the shape variables before a statistical analysis, especially to obtain something like LDA scores.  LDA scores are statistical transformation that distort Procrustes distances among observations, meaning they do not convey shape difference.  (The distances among observations are statistic distances, which might be associated with group association.) To transform variables this way and then use them as data in another analysis is statistical chicanery that is sure to lead to spurious outcomes.

Maximum likelihood on PC scores is fine, but be aware that with shape data, the tendency to have ill-conditioned covariance matrices is great, so methods based on estimating likelihood are likely to lead to interpretive errors.  we discussed this recently: Adams and Collyer.  2018. Multivariate phylogenetic comparative methods: evaluations, comparisons, and recommendations. Systematic biology, 67(1), 14-31.

I do not see any problems with using squared-change parsimony to estimate ancestral character states or any clustering algorithm using Procrustes distances, unless, again  the method requires transforming variables in a strange way.  If you are wondering whether it is okay to build a tree based on Procrustes distances and compare it to a phylogenetic tree based on molecular data, that seems innocuous.  If you are wondering whether shape data can be used to infer models of evolution, that is a much more complicated question to answer, and one I will leave open for discussion.  (I think the answer is “yes” in theory but currently we have limited capacity to do it well.)

Hope that helps!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Russ,

I interpreted Miriam’s comment to mean that problems that depend on the rotation of data are not unique to GM data, as via output from geomorph.  Some of the issues we point out in the reference I gave you is that alternative conclusions can be had from different data rotations (transformations).  For example, perform an analysis to determine the appropriate evolutionary model on Procrustes residuals.  Then do a PCA and perform the same analysis on PC scores.  There should be no difference in model likelihoods, thus no change in conclusion.  Some methods though will give different results/conclusions, as they are not rotation-invariant (and a rotation is one form of transformation).  Miriam added that even if a method is rotation-invariant, there could still be other inferential problems, if an unrealistic model of evolution is assumed.

I believe the point is that these issues are not unique to GM data, not that your question was inappropriate for this forum.  Your question started with “shape variables” but I think she was pointing out that if you asked the same questions with “sad clown variables”, the same concerns would be omnipresent.  At least that was my take.

Mike
